title: The Four Providers
content:
When building AutoPilot for Maestro — the AI that judges whether to approve Claude Code's tool requests — the first question was which model to use.

The obvious answer was: Claude. Fast, good at structured reasoning, costs about a dollar per thousand calls.

Then someone asked: is Claude really the right choice, or just the familiar one?

---

The task is extremely simple. Read a tool name and some arguments. Decide: safe or not?

```
Tool: Bash
Command: rm -rf /Users/joraku/important-files
```

That's a deny. It doesn't take a frontier model to figure that out.

```
Tool: Read  
File: /Users/joraku/project/config.ts
```

That's an allow. Also obvious.

The judgment calls that actually matter — the ambiguous middle ground — might benefit from a capable model. But 80% of decisions are straightforward.

---

So we built support for four providers:

**Claude haiku-4-5** — $0.001/call. Fast, reliable, already trusted for code tasks.

**GPT-4o-mini** — $0.0001/call. Ten times cheaper. For a binary yes/no judgment, the cost difference matters at scale.

**Gemini 1.5 Flash** — $0.00005/call. Twenty times cheaper than Claude. Free tier exists.

**Ollama (local)** — $0.00/call. Runs on your machine. No API key. No data leaves your system. For a yes/no decision, a 1B parameter model running locally is fast enough.

---

The interesting design question was: what's the right default?

We went with Claude haiku as default because it's already in the ecosystem — users building with Claude Code are likely already paying for Anthropic API access. But the option is there to switch.

For users who care about privacy, Ollama is compelling. The hook receives tool names and arguments — potentially sensitive. Routing that through a third-party API is a trust question. Local inference sidesteps it entirely.

For users who want maximum cheapness, Gemini Flash is 20x cheaper than the default.

---

There's a meta-lesson here about feature design.

The temptation when building AI features is to hardcode the best model and call it done. The better approach: make the provider configurable from the start, pick a sensible default, and let users trade off cost/quality/privacy according to their actual needs.

Your "best model" is someone else's "way too expensive" or "sends my data to the wrong cloud".

Make it swappable.
